metadata.title: St Ives stay top despite Stockwood Park defeat in 33-26 thriller
metadata.contentSnippet: A late surge by St Ives saw them secure two bonus points despite a narrow defeat to Stockwood Park.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ives stay top despite Stockwood Park defeat in 33-26 thriller
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A late surge by St Ives saw them secure two bonus points despite a narrow defeat to Stockwood Park. The 33-26 loss in the top-of-the-table clash means the Bulls remain in first place. The match was highly anticipated, and both teams delivered in a closely contested game. Park gained the early advantage, capitalising on a turnover to take the lead. However, Ives quickly levelled the score with a driving maul allowing George Collet to cross the line. As the match progressed, a defensive error by Ives saw them defending a 5-metre scrum. Despite initial resistance, Park managed to break through and extend their lead. The Bulls retaliated, with Oliver Giglio creating an opportunity for Elliot Mortimer, who was stopped just short of the line. Oliver Giglio (Image: St Ives RUFC) Henri Cole supported and finished the move, adding another try for Ives. Approaching half-time, the hosts increased the pressure and managed to cross the line again, bringing the half-time score to 21-14 in favour of Park. The second half saw Ives struggling with possession, leading to another Park try. The home side capitalised on another turnover, increasing their lead to 19 points. Despite the deficit, Ives demonstrated resilience. They fought back with Giglio finishing a well-worked team try. With time running out, the Bulls continued to apply pressure, and in the final play, Jordan Hawes powered through tackles to score. The Director of Rugby, Duncan Williams, reflected on the performance, saying: "We knew it would be a tough challenge as Stockwood are a very well drilled side. "We're disappointed to lose, but happy to leave with 2 bonus points which keeps us top of the table." Ives' determination and late tries ensure they retain their top spot in the league.

news.title: Hunts man due in court accused of employee theft and fraud offences named
news.content: A Huntingdonshire man is due to appear in court accused of a string of fraud and theft offences. Matthew Stokes, 35, of Liberator Road, Ramsey, is accused of fraud by false representation and theft by an employee. His first hearing is due to take place on November 5 at Cambridge Magistrates' Court. He is alleged to have spent £935.83 on personal items using a company credit card while on leave between August 21 and September 2, knowing the transactions were unauthorised and intending to make financial gain. He is also accused of stealing an Apple iPhone worth £285, a Lenovo laptop worth £478 and several tools, including a drill set. The items belonged to water treatment supplier Prodose Ltd and were allegedly stolen between September 2 and October 14. Between November 13 and December 8, Mr Stokes is accused of stealing tools valued at £2,109.18 from Riverside Waste Machinery Ltd. A further fraud charge alleges that he used or permitted the use of company credit cards for unauthorised transactions totalling £412.41 between October 6 and December 8. All the offences are alleged to have taken place in Huntingdon.

metadata.title: St Ives 2nd XV fight back from 19-14 down to beat Cantabrigian 36-19
metadata.contentSnippet: St Ives 2nd XV claimed their first home victory of the season this weekend.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ives 2nd XV fight back from 19-14 down to beat Cantabrigian 36-19
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Ives 2nd XV claimed their first home victory of the season this weekend. The team secured a 36-19 win over Cantabrigian 2s on Saturday afternoon, with a standout second-half performance. Despite a promising start, St Ives found themselves trailing at half-time, with Cantabs opening the scoring with an early try. The home side answered back with a try from Tommy Newman, converted by Matthew Millar, levelling the scores. James Inman added another try, with Millar's conversion giving St Ives a 14-5 advantage. However, Cantabs responded with two converted tries, taking a 19-14 lead into the break. The second half saw a rejuvenated St Ives side take control of the game. Josh Taylor's try shortly after the restart cut the deficit, and the hosts never looked back. The forwards provided a solid platform for the backs to exploit, leading to a series of impressive attacking plays. Jamie Smith and Jamie Pickervance both crossed the line, with Millar landing his third conversion, extending St Ives' lead. As Cantabs struggled to cope with the relentless pressure, Jeremy Irons sealed the win with his first try for the club. Captain Ben Peach praised the team's determination: "It was by no means an easy game, one that was a battle at the beginning, but after half-time we showed great passages of ball movement." His words encapsulated St Ives' comeback, having trailed 19-14 at the interval, they shut out Cantabs in the second half and ran in four unanswered tries. Special recognition was given to Tom Graves for his exceptional performance, earning him the Man of the Match award. The win, built on resilience, physicality and excellent ball movement, marks a promising start to St Ives' home campaign.

metadata.title: Key report on Hunts car park plans has been received, council confirms
metadata.contentSnippet: A key Capital & Centric report detailing recommended next steps for plans to develop Huntingdonshire car parks has been received, HDC has confirmed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Key report on Hunts car park plans has been received, council confirms
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A key Capital & Centric report detailing recommended next steps for plans to develop Huntingdonshire car parks has been received, the council has confirmed. Plans by developer Capital & Centric and Huntingdonshire District Council to build homes on three large car parks in St Neots, Huntingdon and St Ives sparked fury among residents in August. The plans for the St Neots Tebbutts Road car park include two five-storey buildings, up to 83 homes and units for independent businesses. After three public consultations and opposition from councillors, MPs and residents, the plans were rumoured to be "highly unlikely" to go ahead. St Neots residents turned out to the Market Square for the public consultation on Tebbutts Road car park (Image: Emily Stevens) But according to the HDC website, no formal decision has been made on the project yet and it is effectively on pause pending the Gateway 1 report. The report, prepared by Capital & Centric, contains information, plans and drawings informing HDC of the work so far. It will also include recommendations on next steps and future work to enable the council to make an informed decision on the project. The report was expected by the end of September, but it has not yet been released to the public. HDC told The Hunts Post it had received the report and was reviewing it. A spokesperson for HDC said: "The council has received the Capital & Centric Gateway 1 report and is currently reviewing it to ensure factual accuracy, identify any commercially sensitive information, and confirm that it meets the publication requirements agreed with Capital & Centric. "This review process is a normal and established part of the council's approach to publishing reports and information. "To ensure openness and transparency, the council intends to publish the report alongside a council commentary note, setting out the evidence considered and key findings. "Publication of these documents reflects the council's commitment to accountability and providing stakeholders with access to the information that has informed its considerations." Councillors unanimously backed a review after a council document showed that £1,058,720 had been spent on early-stage design and planning work between January and July 2026.

metadata.title: UK flights among 6 planes inspected after suspected bomb threats
metadata.contentSnippet: Four European passenger planes, including flights from London Heathrow and Manchester, face bomb threat inspections.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: UK flights among 6 planes inspected after suspected bomb threats
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six passenger planes across Europe, including two UK departures, are being inspected following suspected bomb threats. A flight from London Heathrow to Warsaw-Chopin Airport was diverted to Warsaw-Modlin Airport in Poland on Tuesday, temporarily closing the airport. Another flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as scheduled and was subsequently inspected by authorities. Elsewhere in Europe, a Ryanair flight from Manchester to Murcia in southern Spain was also subject to a bomb threat, while Bulgarian media reported a flight from Israel to Sofia received a threat via email before landing. The diverted flight, operated by Polish carrier LOT, was carrying 118 people and led to a partial closure of the airport. The affected area remained closed while the rest of the airport resumed operations. SAS confirmed its Copenhagen to Warsaw flight landed safely and all passengers disembarked. Francisco Lucas, the Spanish government’s delegate in the Murcia region, said 121 people were on board the Ryanair flight. He added that the plane was being inspected and security protocol was underway. Murcia-Corvera Airport’s fire brigade was also mobilised. In Bulgaria, Lyubomir Nikolov, chief secretary of the Ministry of Interior, said counter-terrorism teams were examining the aircraft for explosives. These incidents follow a separate event on Monday involving a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Budapest, which was forced to make an emergency landing after a bomb threat. Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found. Sources have also told the BBC that two Ryanair flights, one from Lisbon and the other from Dublin, were searched following anonymous tips regarding potential bomb threats. Flight cancellations can quickly turn travel plans upside down, but passengers are not without rights when journeys are disrupted. Under UK law, airlines are required to provide care and assistance in the event of a cancelled flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption. The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has clarified what travellers are entitled to, including accommodation, meals, and transport between the airport and hotel if re-routed to the following day. The CAA said: "The airline must provide you with these items until it is able to fly you to your destination, no matter how long the delay lasts or what has caused it." If airlines are unable to arrange assistance due to large-scale disruption, passengers are advised to organise their own accommodation and transport and reclaim the costs later. The CAA said: "If you end up paying for things yourself, keep every receipt and do not spend more than is reasonable. "Airlines are unlikely to refund you for things like luxury hotels or alcohol. "Some will provide guidance on reasonable costs." Travellers must also be given the choice between a full refund for unused parts of their ticket or an alternative flight. Compensation may be available depending on the cause of the cancellation. The CAA said: "Disruptions caused by things like extreme weather, airport or air traffic control employee strikes or other ‘extraordinary circumstances’ are not eligible for compensation." Compensation is also dependent on the notice given and the timing of the replacement flight. The CAA said: "If you received less than seven days’ notice of the cancellation, you can claim compensation based on the timings of the alternative flight. "If your new flight departs no more than one hour before the scheduled time of your original flight and your new flight arrives less than two hours after the scheduled time of your original flight, you are not entitled to financial compensation." More detailed information on entitlements and compensation can be found on the CAA website. Have you ever claimed compensation from a flight being cancelled or delayed? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: £50,000 earners face major tax change this week HMRC explains what happens next
metadata.contentSnippet: HMRC has issued five important reminders to sole traders earning over £50,000 ahead of the November 7 Making Tax Digital quarterly update deadline.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £50,000 earners face major tax change this week HMRC explains what happens next
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sole traders and landlords earning more than £50,000 have just days left to submit their second Making Tax Digital update, with HMRC clearing up five common mistakes ahead of the deadline. Thousands of sole traders and landlords face another important tax deadline this week, as HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) reminds people to submit their second Making Tax Digital (MTD) quarterly update by Saturday, November 7. The requirement applies to sole traders and landlords earning more than £50,000, with the new digital reporting system becoming mandatory for them from April 6, 2026. But after the first quarterly update was submitted in August, HMRC says it has been answering a number of common questions and misconceptions about what people need to do next. HMRC has now highlighted five things customers should know before submitting their latest figures - including whether they need to pay tax, what happens if they make a mistake and whether they can leave their submission until Saturday. One of the biggest misconceptions is that a quarterly update is effectively another tax return. HMRC has stressed that this is not the case. An MTD quarterly update is simply a summary of income and expenses from self-employment and property, which must be submitted using compatible software. There is no tax calculation involved and, importantly, no payment is due when the update is sent. Customers' overall tax position will only be calculated when they submit their tax return for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. Anyone who successfully submitted their first quarterly update in August does not need to contact HMRC again for reassurance that it has been received. Instead, customers can check their submission history whenever they want by logging into their HMRC online account or checking through their Making Tax Digital software. HMRC says there is no need to call or use webchat simply to confirm that an update has gone through. Another concern is that Making Tax Digital means customers must purchase complicated or expensive accounting packages. HMRC says there are several recognised software options available to suit different circumstances. These include: Customers can find guidance on choosing Making Tax Digital-compatible software on GOV.UK . Making Tax Digital is designed to allow customers to keep their financial records up to date throughout the year. If someone spots a mistake in a digital record, they should correct it as soon as possible. The correction will then be reflected in their next quarterly update. This means customers do not need to resend an earlier quarterly update simply because they have discovered an error. With less than a week to go until the second quarterly update deadline for Making Tax Digital, make sure you're prepared. ⏰ If you’re a sole trader or landlord with a combined turnover of over £50,000, you need to send your second quarterly update by 7 November. Act now. ⬇️ https://t.co/ZK0DK3dB8I — HM Revenue & Customs (@HMRCgovuk) November 1, 2026 The second quarterly update deadline falls on a Saturday this year, but HMRC has confirmed customers can submit their figures either before or on November 7. The tax authority is encouraging people to get their updates sent as early as possible following the end of the reporting period. Anyone who needs help is encouraged to contact HMRC during the week, when its full phone service is available. However, phone support will also be available through the Self Assessment helpline on Saturday, November 7, between 9am and 3pm, for customers who need assistance with submitting their quarterly update. Business-as-usual webchat services will be available from 8am to 4pm. The Agent Dedicated Line will not be available on the Saturday. Tax agents can instead contact the Self Assessment helpline on 0300 200 3310. Recommended reading: Craig Ogilvie, HMRC's Director of Making Tax Digital, said: "Thousands of sole traders and landlords have already successfully sent their first quarterly update, and we want the second to be just as straightforward. “As the next deadline approaches, we’re helping customers prepare with confidence by answering common questions about MTD and highlighting the support available. "Customers can send their update any time before 7 November and I would encourage them to do so as early as possible to ensure they have everything in place before the deadline." Customers can check whether they qualify on GOV.UK. More information about the requirements, deadlines and support available can be found in HMRC's Making Tax Digital for Income Tax guidance . Making Tax Digital for Income Tax became mandatory for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income above £50,000 from April 6, 2026. However, the rules are being extended to more people over the next two years. The planned timetable is: There are some exemptions, including for people who are digitally excluded.

metadata.title: Holidaymaker's horror as 'refund' from Ryanair turned out to be £900 scam
metadata.contentSnippet: A holidaymaker who complained online about rain-soaked seats on a Ryanair flight was scammed out of £900 after fraudsters offered fake compensation.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Holidaymaker's horror as 'refund' from Ryanair turned out to be £900 scam
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A holidaymaker was scammed out of £900 after complaining online about soaking wet seats on a flight. Sharon Morrell thought she was receiving a £400 compensation payout from Ryanair after rain poured into the cabin before takeoff. The 48-year-old bus driver had booked a four-night package holiday flight from Bristol to Palma, Majorca, alongside her husband and two children on Saturday, October 24. Mrs Morrell said 11 seats near the open aircraft door were left sitting in puddles following heavy downpours. A holidaymaker who complained online about rain-soaked seats on a Ryanair flight was scammed out of £900 after fraudsters offered fake compensation. (Image: Kennedy News and Media) Cabin crew handed passengers paper towels from the toilet to mop up the water themselves before departure, she claimed. Mrs Morrell said: "We were waiting on the stairs for everyone to board the plane, so we were getting soaked then as well. "Obviously Ryanair can't help if there's downpours. "So we got inside the plane and the seats on the left and right side were soaking wet. "Even the seats behind were soaking too. "There were 11 overall that were soaked. "This was all our family's seats and the people behind us. "They weren't just a little bit wet - there were puddles." She said passengers were expected to sit on wet chairs for a two-hour flight, adding: "There was definitely an inch of water. "I said to the staff 'are we expected to just sit on this? This is ridiculous.' "They said 'we'll sort it out in a minute, just get seated so we can get everyone boarded.'" After arriving in Majorca, the mother-of-two shared her frustration on social media. She was shocked when an unknown caller rang her shortly afterwards claiming to represent the airline's compensation team. The caller offered £200 each for her and her husband, and instructed her to download two mobile phone apps to transfer the money safely. Mrs Morrell said: "He said 'no problem, and we can compensate you £200 each for me and my husband for what's happened.' "He sounded genuine." She followed the instructions, only to see funds flowing out of her account instead of coming in. Mrs Morrell said: "I said 'why are there payments leaving my account when it should be the other way around?' "He said 'it's normal process and it's actually payments we're putting into your account.' "He was so clever." The scammer asked for her account balance when payments were declined, prompting her to hang up as transactions totalling £900 went through to Kenya. Mrs Morrell is now disputing the transactions with her bank and warned others against falling for similar traps. She said: "It's so easy to be sucked in and I just can't believe how easy it is to get scammed. "Anybody can fall for these scams. It's my own fault, I got sucked into this." Ryanair said rainwater entered the cabin during boarding due to Storm Boelo. A spokesperson for the airline said: "Due to adverse weather conditions (Storm Boelo) during boarding at Bristol on 24 Oct, a small number of seats near the aircraft door became damp from rainwater entering the cabin. "Crew assisted affected passengers by wiping down the seats and this flight operated normally from Bristol to Palma de Mallorca."

metadata.title: Face of second robber who stole child's bicycle in 'nasty attack'
metadata.contentSnippet: A second robber has been jailed for more than four years for attacking a group of boys in Peterborough and stealing a bicycle.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Face of second robber who stole child's bicycle in 'nasty attack'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A second robber has been jailed for more than four years for attacking a group of boys in Peterborough and stealing a bicycle. Imran Ali, 41, was jailed for 50 months at Cambridge Crown Court on Monday (November 2). The sentence comes after he was found guilty of robbery and two counts of attempted robbery. Together with Declan Hyland, 29, and another man they ambushed the youngsters at around 5pm on April 18. They blocked the path of the teenage boys, two of whom were on bikes and the third a scooter, between Ivatt Way and Bourges Boulevard. They then pushed the boys off the bikes and repeatedly punched them, using keys held within their knuckles as improvised weapons. The boys tried to defend themselves, but Ali managed to ride off on one of the bikes - a Carrera worth about £600. He was closely followed by Hyland, who shouted an insult at the boys as he fled. Declan Hyland was sentenced to five years in prison at the same court (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) The victims received minor injuries, including cuts caused by the keys that were used as weapons. Detectives reviewed CCTV footage from the area resulting in Ali, of no known address, being identified and arrested. A media appeal was circulated with images of the two other men, resulting in Hyland being identified and arrested. The third man was not identified. Hyland, of no known address, admitted robbery and two counts of attempted robbery. On 12 October at the same court he was jailed for five years. DC George Corney said: "This was a nasty attack on three teenage boys that understandably left them extremely shaken. “For three men to attack and rob a group of young boys, who admirably tried to defend themselves, really is cowardly. “I’d like to thank the public for helping us identify one of the perpetrators and therefore bringing them to justice." metadata.title: Knife attacker thought victim, 17, was 'devil', court told
metadata.contentSnippet: A witness to a stabbing on a DLR train at Pontoon Dock told police she believed the attacker had a "psychotic episode", a court heard.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knife attacker thought victim, 17, was 'devil', court told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A witness to a stabbing on a DLR train told police she believed the attacker had a "psychotic episode" and thought his victim was "the devil", a court heard. Isaiah Idris, then aged 17, was attacked on a DLR train in London in the early hours of November 1 last year, Cambridge Crown Court was told. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to an incident on an LNER train in Huntingdon, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one relating to the incident on the DLR train. Earlier this month, Williams pleaded guilty to 10 counts of wounding with intent relating to the LNER train incident, the wounding with intent of a man at Pontoon Dock DLR station in the early hours of November 1 and to the wounding with intent of a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31, as well as a number of other offences. In a video-recorded interview played to jurors on November 3, a witness who was on the train said that the attacker "was specifically targeting a boy". She said: "There was nobody to help, we were very much on our own. "We didn't have anything to defend us. "It was a very scary moment." The witness added that it appeared to her that the attacker had "a psychotic episode". She said: "He was seeing things that weren't clear to the rest of us. "The attacker for some reason thought that this boy was the devil and wanted to harm him." The witness added that the attack was "completely out of nowhere". Judge Mr Justice Calver earlier told jurors that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question, but they must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals when he carried out the attacks. The trial continues.

metadata.title: Eight sieges for every battle: new exhibition reveals Civil War reality
metadata.contentSnippet: Sieges, not battles, take centre stage in a new exhibition in Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Eight sieges for every battle: new exhibition reveals Civil War reality
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sieges, not battles, take centre stage in a new exhibition in Huntingdon. The Cromwell Museum's latest display, Besieged: Sieges of the Civil War, reveals the overlooked reality of the English Civil Wars. While just 28 major battles took place in England between 1642 and 1648, 189 locations were besieged, and more than 1,000 fortified sites could be found across the British Isles. Stuart Orme, curator of the Cromwell Museum, said: "When people think of the Civil Wars they tend to think of the great battles like Edgehill, Naseby, or Worcester, but there were eight sieges for every one of these. "Places all over Britain and Ireland were fortified and then besieged as part of this brutal conflict, dragging many thousands of ordinary people into the front line of the conflict and leaving scars on the landscape and many of our historic buildings that can still be seen today." The exhibition, which runs from November 3, 2026, to April 4, 2027, explores why so many towns and castles were fortified, how earthwork defences were constructed, and how siege tactics developed throughout the conflict. It also examines the roles of those involved, from engineers and soldiers to civilians and women who defended their homes. Visitors can view original artefacts including siege plans, musket balls, a cannonball from the siege of Sheffield Castle, and a scale model of Earith Bulwark. The only surviving Civil War siege helmet in the UK is also on display. Case studies of key locations feature throughout the exhibition, including Oxford, Bristol, Leicester, Skipton Castle, Pontefract, and Hull. Entry is free, though donations are welcome. The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday from 10am to 3.30pm. More information is available at cromwellmuseum.org.

metadata.title: Huntingdon MP backs winter coat campaign after Rotary St Ives raises £2,000
metadata.contentSnippet: A charity campaign helping children stay warm through winter is being championed in Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon MP backs winter coat campaign after Rotary St Ives raises £2,000
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A charity campaign helping children stay warm through winter is being championed in Huntingdon. Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty recently joined children’s charity Coats4Kids in Parliament to support its latest winter campaign, which aims to ensure no pupil arrives at school without an adequate winter coat. Mr Obese-Jecty praised the work of Rotary St Ives, which has raised more than £2,000 to fund the rollout of the scheme across seven primary schools. He said: "Arriving at school cold or wet is an immediate barrier to a child's readiness to learn. "Coats4Kids provides a practical solution that makes a real difference to young people across our communities. "This initiative succeeds because of dedicated local champions, and I want to express my thanks to Rotary St Ives." Of the 10 schools currently participating in the scheme across the Huntingdon constituency, seven are supported through the club’s fundraising. Nationally, Coats4Kids has delivered more than 11,000 brand-new winter coats to children in need. The charity works with school safeguarding and pastoral staff, who identify pupils requiring support. Children are then given a digital voucher to select a new coat online, which is delivered directly to their home. This approach removes the stigma of second-hand clothing and avoids the need for schools to store or distribute items. Mr Obese-Jecty encouraged wider participation. He said: "By raising over £2,000 and backing seven of our primary schools, St Ives Rotary has shown what community spirit looks like in action. "I strongly encourage any local schools not yet taking part to get in touch with the charity and get involved." Coats4Kids has recently expanded its scheme to include secondary schools, extending support to older students as winter approaches. Schools and community members interested in taking part can contact Coats4Kids directly for more information.

metadata.title: St Neots Hockey Club's second teams snatch late wins after first-team defeats
metadata.contentSnippet: St Neots Hockey Club experienced a weekend of mixed fortunes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots Hockey Club's second teams snatch late wins after first-team defeats
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Neots Hockey Club experienced a weekend of mixed fortunes. Both first teams suffered frustrating away defeats, while the men's and women's second teams claimed dramatic late victories. The men's first team slipped to a narrow 3-2 defeat at Wisbech Town. St Neots made the perfect start when Andrew Pope fired them ahead after just two minutes, but Wisbech gradually wrestled control of the contest, scoring either side of half-time before adding a third seven minutes into the second period. Sam Evans set up a tense finish with a goal in the final minute, but the visitors were unable to find the equaliser their performance arguably deserved. The women's first team also endured a disappointing afternoon, losing 3-1 away at St Ives 2s. Two early goals put the home side firmly in command before Marie Quintilla halved the deficit on 25 minutes. However, St Ives restored their two-goal advantage midway through the second half to secure the points. There was much more to celebrate for the club's second teams, who both demonstrated impressive resilience to secure one-goal victories. The men's second team twice responded to setbacks before snatching all three points in a thrilling 3-2 victory over St Ives 2s. Andrew Chin gave Saints an early lead, only for St Ives 2s to equalise before the interval. Phil McMorris restored the advantage early in the second half, but St Ives levelled again with eight minutes remaining. Just as the match appeared destined to end in a draw, Brad Forsdick struck in the 69th minute to seal a deserved victory. The women's second team also enjoyed late celebrations after edging out Cambridge Nomads 2s 2-1. Rebecca Hindle broke the deadlock shortly after the restart, but Nomads responded ten minutes later. Saints continued to press and were rewarded three minutes from time when Ness Wilson found the winner.

metadata.title: 'Cowardly' driver fled scene of crash which left passenger in coma
metadata.contentSnippet: A "cowardly" dangerous driver has been jailed after causing a crash in Peterborough that left his passenger with a brain injury.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Cowardly' driver fled scene of crash which left passenger in coma
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "cowardly" dangerous driver has been jailed after causing a crash that left his passenger with a brain injury. Nicusor Ionescu was speeding down Eastfield Road, Peterborough, at about 12.55pm on September 6. He lost control of his Mercedes and collided with a tree before running away from the scene. The 27-year-old hid behind a nearby van, leaving his front-seat passenger trapped in the vehicle with serious injuries. Members of the public who witnessed the collision chased Ionescu and detained him, before officers arrived and arrested him. Ionescu’s 27-year-old passenger suffered a brain injury, multiple fractures and was in a medically induced coma for two weeks as a result of the crash. At Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday (October 28), Ionescu, of Granville Street, Peterborough, was jailed for two years. He admitting to causing serious injury by dangerous driving, using a motor vehicle without insurance, and using a motor vehicle without a valid license. Sentencing, Judge Andrew Hurst, commented on the fact that the victim is now unable to work and is "confined by his own fragile mental health". Detective Constable Lauren Byrne, from the force’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit, said: "Firstly my thoughts go out to the victim and his family. "This crash has had an extensive impact on them all and I wish the victim a speedy recovery. "This was a serious, but completely preventable crash, caused by Ionescu’s careless and reckless driving. "The impact of the collision goes far beyond the victim’s physical injuries - he will likely suffer from the ongoing emotional and psychological impact, especially as he is unable to work or continue his life as it was prior to the crash. "The fact Ionescu tried to flee the scene is cowardly and shows his lack of remorse and compassion for the victim, so I am pleased he is now behind bars and will be held accountable for his actions."

metadata.title: Knife attacker 'spat at' police detention officer on train, court told
metadata.contentSnippet: The man accused of a knife attack on an LNER train in Huntingdon last year "spat at" a police officer on a train travelling to Peterborough, a court heard.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knife attacker 'spat at' police detention officer on train, court told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The man accused of a knife attack on board an LNER train in Huntingdon last year "spat at" a police officer on a train travelling to Peterborough, a court has heard. Multiple people were injured on the service travelling to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. Earlier this month, Williams pleaded guilty to 10 counts of wounding with intent relating to the incident on the LNER train, the wounding with intent of a man at Pontoon Dock DLR station in the early hours of November 1 and to the wounding with intent of a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31, as well as a number of other offences. At Cambridge Crown Court on November 3, Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC told jurors that a man, agreed by the prosecution and defence to be Williams, 'spat at' a passenger, Jordan Morley, on a train travelling to Peterborough at around 8am on November 1, 2025. Mr Morley, a police detention officer at Islington Custody, was on his way home from work and had boarded the 7.16am service at King's Cross St Pancras, the court heard in a statement read out by the prosecution. He "felt what I would describe as a spray of spittle" as he sat on the train which had just stopped at Hitchin, the court heard. The court heard how Mr Morley was "almost in disbelief that he had spat at him". He had no previous interaction with the male who spat at him, the court was told. Mr Morley exited the train at Biggleswade and sent a text message to British Transport Police at 8.18am on November 1, 2025, the court heard. Williams has pleaded guilty to common assault on a Thameslink train travelling between London and Biggleswade on November 1. The trial continues.

metadata.title: Latest on sudden closure of Hunts nursery after 'safeguarding incident'
metadata.contentSnippet: Further details surrounding the sudden closure of The Anchor Nursery and Pre-School in King's Ripton, near Huntingdon, have emerged.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Latest on sudden closure of Hunts nursery after 'safeguarding incident'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Further details surrounding the sudden closure of a nursery in Huntingdonshire have emerged. The Anchor Nursery and Pre-School in King's Ripton, near Huntingdon, closed on October 23 after Ofsted suspended its registration. Golden Apples Nurseries, which operates the site, has since confirmed a "safeguarding incident" occurred at the site on October 21. A spokesperson said: "Immediate action was taken in line with safeguarding procedures, and we continue to work closely with the relevant authorities. "The safety and wellbeing of every child in our care remains our highest priority." Although the education watchdog said it does not comment on individual providers, its guidance on suspension is clear. Ofsted will suspend a provider's registration if it "believes a child or children may be at risk of harm". However, suspension is not a final finding of guilt or fault but an interim measure designed to safeguard children. The minimum suspension period for a childcare provider's registration is six weeks, which allows Ofsted time to investigate concerns. In a fresh update on Tuesday (November 3), Cambridgeshire Police said it was aware of the incident. A spokesperson said: "We are aware of an incident at the nursery, no crimes were identified and we have left investigations with LADO." Cambridgeshire County Council added: "We understand this must be unsettling for affected families. "A member of our Early Years Team has attended the nursery to support the management of the situation and provide parents and carers with further information about support available. "We have also issued letters to parents and carers detailing where they can find support with alternative childcare places." Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: Further details behind closure of much-loved village pub emerge
metadata.contentSnippet: For months now mystery has shrouded the fate of The Black Bull in Brampton which closed its doors without explanation.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Further details behind closure of much-loved village pub emerge
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: For months now mystery has shrouded the fate of a popular village pub in Huntingdonshire which closed its doors without explanation. The Black Bull, on Church Road, in Brampton, announced it had closed "for the foreseeable future" in August. The 16th century venue was run by Malcolm Beswick and is operated by the UK's largest pub company, Stonegate. Now, ex-staff have come forward to reveal further details surrounding the watering hole's sudden closure. They claim "things took a turn for the worst" in February when the pub began "running out of stock", including soft drinks and kitchen supplies. "The place wasn't really managed, if I'm honest, it was all over the place," one ex-employee, who asked to remain anonymous, told The Hunts Post. However, stock would turn out to be the least of the pub's worries as a subsequent Food Standard's Agency inspection revealed. The premises was slapped with a zero food hygiene rating by the independent government body following a review of the site on May 6. It said "major improvement" was necessary in areas including "management of food safety" as well as "cleanliness and conditions of facilities and building". "The kitchen hasn't had a deep clean in a number of years and we were finding food that was out of date," a former employee said. "We once served a whole table with mouldy Yorkshire puddings which had been prepped the week before. "The hygiene was really bad, staff would go outside, smoke a cigarette, go back in and not wash their hands." Former staff said the hygiene rating forced the closure of the kitchen, but claim that despite this it was still not professionally deep-cleaned. "It was quite uncertain and a lot of us were message each other about the future of the pub," they added. "We didn't know if the pub was going to be open and if we were going to have our jobs back which caused a lot of stress." Describing the culture at The Black Bull, one ex-employee even claims they often had no designated break unless they requested one. Mr Beswick revealed the pub would close "permanently" in a WhatsApp message sent to staff on August 13. The correspondence, seen by this newspaper and verified by two sources, confirmed the reason behind the closure in a bid to "avoid speculation". "Thank you all for your patience, I'm afraid we have to close permanently. "To avoid speculation I found out today that the brewery filed a bankruptcy petition over a £21,000 debt for buying out of tie. "I'm afraid I dropped the ball on that and it has cost everything including sadly your jobs," it added. According to The Gazette, a petition to declare Mr Beswick bankrupt was filed at Cambridge County Court on March 16. The application was lodged by the creditor Unique Pub Property Limited, which is a subsidiary of Stonegate. A bankruptcy order has since come into effect and will automatically discharge on June 10 next year, the Individual Insolvency Registers shows. In a statement, Stonegate said it is unable to comment on "any alleged legal or financial matters concerning individual third parties". A spokesperson said: "We are actively seeking a new tenant to take on the Black Bull, Brampton. "The Black Bull is a valued local pub with an important role to play in the community, and our priority is to secure the right operator to take the business forward. "We are keen to see the pub reopen as soon as possible and are actively seeking a new tenant who can build on its potential and re-establish it as a thriving venue." Mr Beswick has been approached for comment. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk or newsdesk@huntspost.co.uk

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire joins major UK trial testing new Alzheimer’s treatments
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough have enrolled their first participants in a major UK trial for Alzheimer’s treatments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire joins major UK trial testing new Alzheimer’s treatments
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough have enrolled their first participants in a major UK trial for Alzheimer’s treatments. The study, supported by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust (CPFT), is part of the AD-SMART trial—a national effort to accelerate the search for effective therapies. Dr Ben Underwood, director of research and development at CPFT and the trial’s local principal investigator, said: "We are delighted to welcome Angela and Steve to join the trial with us at CPFT and hope this research will directly benefit them and countless others living with Alzheimer’s disease. "Our research would not be possible without people like them coming forward to help us. "We will support them throughout their research journey and hope that many others will join to help test promising dementia treatments and ensure the most successful ones can be brought to NHS clinics as soon as possible." The AD-SMART trial is the first of its kind to test multiple drugs at the same time, beginning with two medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Angela and Steve Bucksey, residents from Cambridgeshire who joined the study, said: "Following Angela’s diagnosis, we decided to take part in a study at a local friendly research unit without having to travel into London, and it feels good to be doing something about it." The trial will involve up to 20 NHS sites over the next 12 to 18 months, with more than 30 planned in total. Researchers aim to recruit 1,200 participants across the UK. Researchers expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030. Individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of Alzheimer’s who wish to take part can contact the CPFT Research team at RandD@cpft.nhs.uk or call 01223 219753. For more information on dementia research and other clinical trial opportunities, visit Join Dementia Research.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: John Lewis Christmas advert divides fans with some saying it ‘missed the mark’
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: John Lewis' 2026 Christmas advert has divided viewers, with some calling it "lovely" and others saying it "missed the mark." The advert was released on November 3 and stars Dame Kristin Scott Thomas as Gloria, a grandmother hosting her family in London on Christmas Eve. When her grandchildren Freddie and Maggie disrupt her study, Gloria brings down Pickles, a vintage pull-along Little Snoopy toy voiced by Paul Whitehouse, to entertain them. Pickles springs to life and encourages Gloria to do more than give cash, leading her on a tuk-tuk journey to John Lewis. On Christmas morning, the children are given a key instead of money, unlocking Gloria’s study to reveal a transformed "Gran Cave" filled with lights, disco balls, and a turntable. Set to a Sam Fender cover of You Can’t Always Get What You Want by The Rolling Stones, the advert aims to capture the magic of Christmas with a personal touch. The song was recorded with children from John Spence Community High School and a brass section with the Easington Colliery Band. Proceeds from the single will support the Teenage Cancer Trust and Action for Children. Public reaction to the advert has been mixed, with some viewers praising its heartwarming message and others feeling underwhelmed. One YouTube commenter wrote: "Love the heart and message behind this, it just took a bit of time to get to the point! Worth sticking with though." Another viewer said: "The sentiment is there but I’m used to crying into my morning coffee with the John Lewis Christmas adverts, not this year." A third added: "I like the sentiment, but unfortunately was a miss for me again this year." However, others were more positive. One fan wrote: "My fave John Lewis ad in a while, wanted to cry for Pickles." Another said: "Lovely ad, I know my child would love that room. "And so great that the soundtrack will bring children safety and happiness by supporting Action for Children." What are your thoughts on the 2026 John Lewis Christmas advert? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire police officers added to barred list doubled in last year
metadata.contentSnippet: The number of Cambridgeshire police officers who were added to the College of Policing's barred list doubled in the last year, new data shows.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire police officers added to barred list doubled in last year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The number of Cambridgeshire police officers who were added to the barred list doubled in the last year, according to new data. College of Policing figures show 20 Cambridgeshire officers were barred in 2025/26, up from 10 the previous year and three in 2023/24. The College of Policing is an independent body for everyone working in policing. Introduced in 2017, the barred list names officers, special constables and staff dismissed from policing after investigations. Nine Cambridgeshire officers were barred in 2022/23, compared with two in 2021/22 and three in 2020/21. This means more Cambridgeshire Police officers were added to the barred list in 2025/26 than in any other year since 2020. Nationally, 757 police officers were banned from serving after they were sacked for breaching professional standards in the year to the end of March 2026, up from 735 in 2024/25 and 594 in 2023/24. The College of Policing said on November 3 that it was the highest annual total since the barred list began. Assistant Chief Constable Arman Mathieson, director of operational standards at the College of Policing, said: “Policing is built on trust and these figures show we will not hesitate to act when that trust is broken. “757 officers have been removed and barred from ever serving again, including those who retired or resigned while under investigation. “This represents 0.5% of all serving officers, with the vast majority of officers serving with courage, professionalism and integrity. “We all deserve a service that roots out those who fall short. "Where standards are breached, we will find out and we will act. “Since the barred list was introduced in December 2017, 3,591 regular officers have been added in total, with the pace of dismissals accelerating markedly: 757 officers were barred last year alone, more than in any single year since the list began and over twice the annual average of the preceding four years.”

metadata.title: £120,000 conservation project launched to protect historic Houghton Mill
metadata.contentSnippet: Conservation work is underway to protect a historic watermill in Huntingdonshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £120,000 conservation project launched to protect historic Houghton Mill
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Conservation work is underway to protect a historic watermill in Huntingdonshire. The project aims to safeguard Houghton Mill, one of the country’s few surviving watermills, from the pressures of age, weather, and seasonal flooding. Funding has come from the Wolfson Foundation, contributing to the estimated £120,000 cost of the scheme. Isabel Sedgwick, visitor operations manager at Houghton Mill, said: "Houghton Mill is a remarkable place, and we’re incredibly fortunate to be able to care for a building with such a rich history while keeping it working for visitors today. "This project is about making sure we can continue to share the sights, sounds and stories of the mill for many years to come. "The support from the Wolfson Foundation is helping us tackle some really important repairs and protect the mill’s character for future generations." External Repairs - Houghton Mill (Image: National Trust Images Mike Selby) The first phase of work will address the north and east sides of the mill, following detailed surveys that identified urgent repairs. A key focus will be the conservation of the north lucam, the overhanging timber hoist once used to lift grain into the mill. Specialist craftspeople will stabilise and repair the historic structure using traditional methods. The project will also include roof repairs, replacement of lead flashings, and restoration of weatherboarding, windows, and dormers. A Cambridgeshire-based firm, Brown and Ralph Ltd, is carrying out the work. The conservation is expected to be completed by January 2027, with the mill due to reopen to the public at Easter. Paul Ramsbottom, chief executive at the Wolfson Foundation, said: "Houghton Mill is an important part of our industrial heritage – there has been an active mill on this site for over 1,000 years. "We are pleased that our long-standing partnership with the National Trust can help support this essential restoration."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A mayor has criticised ongoing delays to local government reorganisation in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. Paul Bristow, Mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said the Government has delayed a decision on local government reorganisation in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, with an update now promised next year, leaving months of uncertainty for residents, councillors, and staff. Mr Bristow said: "The Government needs to answer a straightforward question: does it want to change how councils are structured in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, or not?" He called for clarity and urgency, warning that the area risks being left behind while other parts of the country are getting certainty about their future. Mr Bristow said: "If it does, it needs to get on with it. "If it has doubts, it should explain them openly rather than leave people guessing."

metadata.title: Walkers recalls crisps over health concerns as shoppers warned 'do not eat'
metadata.contentSnippet: Walkers Variety Snacks Sharing Box is being recalled over undeclared wheat. Check the affected dates, batch code and refund advice.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Walkers recalls crisps over health concerns as shoppers warned 'do not eat'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Walkers snack sharing box is being recalled over undeclared wheat. PepsiCo is recalling its Walkers Variety Snacks Sharing Box after wheat was left off the outer packaging, creating a possible risk for some people with allergies or coeliac disease. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the affected boxes have best-before dates of November 21, 2026, or January 16, 2027. The alert applies to crisps sold in England, Scotland and Wales. The problem concerns an 85g packet of Monster Munch Giants Roast Beef inside the box, which contains wheat and gluten not declared on the outside of the sharing box. The FSA said: "This product contains gluten making it a possible health risk for anyone with an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or with coeliac disease." Affected boxes weigh 655g and contain six packs of snacks. The batch code to look for on the affected boxes is 107543. Anyone who has bought an affected box and has an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or has coeliac disease, is advised not to eat it. Instead, the FSA says customers can call the PepsiCo Consumer Care Line on 0800 274 777 or visit contact.pepsico.com/walkers to receive a full refund. PepsiCo has issued a point-of-sale notice explaining the recall and what customers should do. The NHS says a food allergy is different from a food intolerance and that allergic reactions can be serious for some people. It advises calling 999 if, for example, someone's lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or they are struggling to breathe. If someone having a serious allergic reaction has an adrenaline auto-injector or nasal spray, the NHS says to use it immediately and call 999 even if they seem to be feeling better. Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which eating gluten causes the immune system to attack the body's own tissues, damaging the small intestine, the NHS says. Symptoms can include diarrhoea, abdominal pain and bloating, and a gluten-free diet helps control symptoms and prevent long-term complications. The FSA explains that a food may be withdrawn from sale when there is a problem that means it should not be sold. A recall is when customers are asked to return the product, rather than it simply being taken off shelves. Food can be withdrawn or recalled because allergy information is missing or incorrect, or because there is another food allergy risk. When there is a food allergy risk, the agency issues an allergy alert.

metadata.title: Knifeman had ‘eyes wide open like he was on something’, court told
metadata.contentSnippet: A knifeman who stabbed 10 people on an LNER train has been described by a 14-year-old boy he stabbed the day before as having ‘eyes wide open like he was on something’, a court heard.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knifeman had ‘eyes wide open like he was on something’, court told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A knifeman who stabbed 10 people on a London-bound train was described by a boy he stabbed the day before as having ‘his eyes wide open like he was on something’, a court heard. Several people were injured on an LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, where CCTV of the knife attack was shown in court. Anthony Williams, 33, denies ten counts of attempted murder relating to the incident. He also denies the attempted murders of three people in Peterborough on October 31, and of a 17-year-old boy at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London in the early hours of November 1. His trial opened at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, October 28. Judge Mr Justice Calver earlier told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question but they must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals when he carried out the attacks. Cambridge Crown Court (Image: LDR) A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, told police in a video-recorded interview played in court on Friday that he was stabbed on Halloween last year. He said he was going to go trick or treating with friends and was walking over a bridge behind an Asda store in Peterborough when a man ‘just pulled out a knife and stabbed me’. He described the person as "this random guy" and said it happened shortly after 7pm as he was walking with a friend, along a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk. "We’ve pretty much got right up close to him as we’re walking past him and he’s pulled out a knife and just stabbed me," the boy said. He added: "I didn’t feel like he was mentally sane. "His eyes were wide open like he was on something." He said the man "shouted something, I don’t know what he said". "I jumped back a little when I saw he was reaching for something and I started running," the boy said. He continued: "He was screaming something. "My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'." He said he and his friend ran and hid in bushes and called the police. Asked what force the man had used, the boy said: "It was strong, like it pushed me back a little bit. "He was using his full force, his arm was fully stretched out." He said the man was dressed in black and he believed the knife was around 10 inches long. A group of police officers stand close to the emergency equipment left behind after an incident at Huntingdon train station (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) The boy’s friend, who also cannot be identified for legal reasons, said the man who he described as a black male had shouted "are you two involved?". In a statement read in court, he said the man "pulled out a large knife" from a rucksack, describing the knife as a "type of zombie knife or Rambo-style knife". Williams is accused of the attempted murders of two others in Peterborough on October 31, Dawid Taborski and William Ogelby. Mr Taborski said in a video interview that he had been on his way to a rave when a man he had never seen before "kept saying are you involved, are you involved?" He said he "didn’t know what he (Williams) was on about, I was really confused" and he initially thought it may have been "a Halloween thing". "As soon as he took that knife out I ran," he added. "It happened so quickly." The scene at Huntingdon train station after the incident last year (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) Detective Constable Ryan Burke said he was on high-visibility foot patrols when Mr Taborski approached him by Charters bar in Peterborough and told him "someone had attempted to stab him but they hadn’t been able to do so". The officer said in a statement that Mr Taborski told him the man had "brandished a long silver blade" and "lunged attempting to stab him". Mr Ogelby told police he had been walking to a cashpoint to get money out when a man walking towards him said "wagwan" to him, which he understood to be a greeting. "I’ve said (it) back and he’s pulled a knife out and tried to stab me three times in my stomach and once in my chest," he said in a video interview played to jurors. He said he ran home "as fast as my legs would carry me" and "checked myself to see if I was bleeding – I wasn’t bleeding". "I thought he was going to kill me," he said. Jurors were shown a photo of Mr Ogelby wearing a jacket which had what prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC described as a "knife cut" to it. The trial continues, with jurors asked to return to court on Monday, November 2.

metadata.title: Hunts Phil to perform songs by composer killed on Somme at Remembrance event
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdonshire Philharmonic, also known as Hunts Phil, are set to perform a Remembrance concert at St Mary’s Church, Godmanchester.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts Phil to perform songs by composer killed on Somme at Remembrance event
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "distinguished" amateur choir in Huntingdonshire will hold a Remembrance event with songs by a composer killed on the Somme. Huntingdonshire Philharmonic, also known as Hunts Phil, will perform at St Mary’s Church, Godmanchester, on Saturday, November 7, at 7.30pm. The first half of the programme will feature six songs from George Butterworth’s A Shropshire Lad, sung by baritone Caleb Richards. Butterworth was killed by a sniper at Pozières on the Somme in August 1916, aged 31. Before leaving for France, he destroyed the manuscripts he was dissatisfied with, fearing he would not come back to revise them, and left the rest to his friend Ralph Vaughan Williams. The rest of the programme includes Vaughan Williams’s Lord, Thou Hast Been Our Refuge, John Ireland’s Greater Love Hath No Man, and Herbert Sumsion’s They That Go Down to the Sea in Ships. The second half is Matthew Coleridge’s Requiem. Classic FM has described it as a modern choral classic. The concert is in the middle of Hunts Phil’s 50th anniversary season, which opened on October 17 to a capacity audience. The choir is conducted by Nicholas Morris.

Charlotte Horobin, chief executive of the chamber, won the President’s Award, while events and training manager Zoë Brennan was highly commended in the Rising Star category. Three member businesses – Paragraf, Welch Group, and Thermoteknix – were also shortlisted for national awards. Charlotte said: "This is the icing on the cake for everything the Chamber has achieved, it reflects the enormous amount of work put in by the whole team. "We’ve been ambitious about strengthening the Chamber, growing the value we provide to the local economy and ensuring the voice of our business community is heard locally, nationally and internationally." Zoë’s commendation recognises her leadership of more than 115 annual business events and her role in the chamber’s recent rebrand and digital transformation. Zoë said: "To receive this recognition on a national stage is an incredible honour. "I've been fortunate to grow my career within an organisation that has given me the confidence, opportunities and support to develop, and I'm so proud to be part of such a passionate team. "What makes this particularly special is knowing that the work we do brings businesses together, creates opportunities and makes a genuine difference to our members. "I'm excited about what we can continue to achieve together." Faye Holland, chair of the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "What an extraordinary moment for our Chamber and our business community. "Charlotte's President's Award is a thoroughly deserved recognition of her vision and transformative leadership. "She has not simply strengthened the organisation; she has reshaped its influence and ability to deliver for businesses across our region."

metadata.title: Burglar jailed after leaving DNA on beer can at Cambs crime scene
metadata.contentSnippet: A burglar who smashed his way into Café Au Chocolat in Cambridge has been jailed after leaving DNA on a beer can at one of the crime scenes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Burglar jailed after leaving DNA on beer can at Cambs crime scene
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A burglar who smashed his way into Cambridgeshire shops has been jailed after leaving DNA on a beer can at one of the crime scenes. Darren Scales, 57, of no fixed address, was jailed for a year at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on Friday, October 30, after admitting four burglaries and three shop thefts. On September 1, Scales smashed through Café Au Chocolat’s front door in Green Street, Cambridge, and stole £150 from the till. He was also caught on CCTV breaking into Custom Ink Tattooing on Victoria Avenue, where he stole a cashbox containing more than £750. On September 30, he carried out another burglary in King’s Parade, stealing £500 worth of vapes. Then, on 15 October, he broke into Waterstones, in Sidney Street, forcing his way into the tills and stealing charity boxes. Darren Scales stole from several shops across Cambridge (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Scales also stole meat and alcohol from Tesco, Marks and Spencer and Co-op on 4 October. He was caught after a beer can left at Café Au Chocolat was found to contain his DNA. PC Samantha Chapman, from the Acquisitive Crime Team, said: "Burglary has a real impact on businesses, from the financial loss to the damage and disruption caused. "In this case, CCTV and a beer can left behind provided valuable evidence. "He is now facing the consequences of his actions with a year behind bars."

metadata.title: Government to proceed with plans for asylum seeker housing in village
metadata.contentSnippet: The government has confirmed it intends to proceed with plans to use Roman Court, in Leverington, near Wisbech, to house asylum seekers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Government to proceed with plans for asylum seeker housing in village
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The government has confirmed it intends to proceed with plans to use a former sheltered living complex to house asylum seekers. In a letter, the Home Office confirmed its decision to use Roman Court, in Leverington, near Wisbech, to house mothers and babies. It comes less than two weeks after a fire ripped through a disused building at the site, which police are investigating as arson. Fenland District Council said the decision "demonstrates a complete disregard for the serious risks the plans pose to public safety, community cohesion and civil unrest." Concerns have been raised about the site which was earmarked as part of government plans to move asylum seekers out of hotels and into longer-term homes. Police continue to investigate a fire which ripped through a disused building at the site (Image: Colin Martin) Cllr Sam Hoy, Fenland District Council portfolio holder for housing, said: "We are extremely alarmed by the Home Office’s decision which has been taken despite extensive evidence from the Council and our partners highlighting serious concerns about the suitability of Roman Court and the risks associated with this proposal. "What is particularly troubling is that the Home Office has chosen to proceed at a time when there has already been significant unrest linked to these plans, including public protests and the fire at the site, which remains the subject of an ongoing police investigation. "These events have demonstrated the strength of local concern and the heightened tensions that exist within the community. "We do not believe those circumstances can simply be dismissed as issues that can be managed through routine arrangements. "Our position remains unchanged. Roman Court is the wrong location for this proposal, and we remain deeply concerned about the impact on both future residents and the wider community. "We will continue to make our objections known to the Home Office and work with our partners to ensure local concerns are heard and appropriately addressed." As the contracted accommodation provider, Serco will be required to demonstrate the site meets legal, regulator and property requirements before occupation. "This will include the relevant safeguarding, welfare, security, fire safety and operational arrangements," the letter reads. "Where site-specific action or mitigation is required, this will be taken forward with Serco and the relevant partners as the site progresses. "The accommodation will not become operational until the applicable requirements have been met, with input from relevant partners sought through the appropriate channels where required." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: No trains between Peterborough or Letchworth and London due to weekend works
metadata.contentSnippet: No trains will run between Peterborough or Letchworth and London for a whole weekend this month due to engineering works.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: No trains between Peterborough or Letchworth and London due to weekend works
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: No trains will run between Peterborough or Letchworth and London later this month due to engineering works. The disruption will take place on Saturday, November 28 and Sunday, November 29, as part of the £1.4 billion East Coast Digital Programme (ECDP), which will replace traditional signals with real-time, in-cab digital signalling. Passengers are advised to check their journeys and expect rail replacement services on affected routes. No Thameslink or Great Northern trains will run between Moorgate, London St Pancras or London King's Cross and Letchworth Garden City or Peterborough all weekend. Rail replacement buses will be operating on the following routes: Most LNER services will start and terminate at Peterborough, with rail replacement coaches connecting customers to Bedford where Thameslink trains will operate to London St Pancras. Ricky Barsby, head of access integration (ECDP) for Network Rail, said: "We have begun to introduce digital in-cab signalling to the East Coast Main Line and we’re getting ready to extend its use to more services. "When all trains operate with digital signalling there will be reliability benefits through less reliance on trackside equipment and better ability to recover from disruption. "We are also taking the opportunity to do other vital engineering work on the track and lineside to improve the reliability of day-to-day services. "We’re sorry to anyone whose journey will be affected. "Those customers who have choice about when they can travel may want to consider travelling on days before or after, which are unaffected by work. "For those who need to travel on the affected weekend, we have plans in place to keep passengers moving." A spokesperson for the train operators said: "We’re working with Network Rail to help passengers plan their journeys while these important upgrades take place. "No trains will be able to run on the East Coast Main Line between Peterborough or Letchworth Garden City and London on November 28 and 29. "Passengers should check before they travel and allow extra time, as services will be significantly altered and rail replacement services will be in operation for many journeys."
