metadata.title: Centrepoint resident welcomes minister to mark new changes to Housing Benefit
metadata.contentSnippet: Centrepoint welcomed the new changes by hosting a visit from Department for Work and Pensions Minister Stephen Timms MP

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Centrepoint resident welcomes minister to mark new changes to Housing Benefit
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Following Centrepoint’s yearlong Make Work Pay campaign, young people in supported housing accommodation will no longer be penalised for working more. For years, a flaw in the benefits system meant that those who tried to work more hours, take on extra shifts or do better paid work were often left financially worse off. Now, new changes to Housing Benefit rules mean residents aged 16-25 will keep more of what they earn.  Around 30,000 young people living in supported housing receive Housing Benefit. Centrepoint welcomed the new changes by hosting a visit from Department for Work and Pensions Minister Stephen Timms MP to one of its East London supported accommodation services.  There, the Minister met Sadaf, a 19-year-old resident who talked about her hopes for the future. Throughout her time with Centrepoint, Sadaf has overcome difficulties but remains committed to her long-term aspiration to study medicine and build a better future for herself. Like many young people transitioning towards independence, Sadaf viewed employment as a positive step towards self-sufficiency. Her intention in seeking work was not only to gain financial independence but also to fund her education and create future opportunities. Sadaf said: "Working made me feel like I was moving forward. I finally felt like I was doing something productive and taking responsibility for my future." However, gaining employment triggered a significant reduction in Sadaf’s Housing Benefit entitlement. The reduction created a substantial gap between her accommodation costs and available income, resulting in rent arrears that eventually approached £5,000. Rather than creating greater financial stability, employment created financial uncertainty.  The impact extended far beyond finances alone. Housing uncertainty affected her future plans, educational opportunities, relationships and overall wellbeing. Now that the system is working better, Sadaf is actively seeking employment again.  She said: "There were times when it felt like working made everything harder, but I still believe education and employment are the way forward for me. I want to build a future where I can support myself, help other people and become the person I've always wanted to be.” Seyi Obakin OBE, Chief Executive Officer at Centrepoint, said: “This is a landmark win for young people, and we commend the government for getting this change over the line.  For too long, young people in supported housing, particularly those at the start of their careers, have had their ambitions blocked by a system that punished them for working harder. "This is what it looks like when the system works for young people, and we hope it creates a smoother transition from benefits into work for them.” An incredible evening was had on Tuesday 13th October at London's Bloomsbury Ballroom for the annual Centrepoint Awards. (Image: devantayj) The event, hosted by broadcaster and long-time Centrepoint supporter Gaby Roslin, celebrated the achievements of inspirational young people who have been supported by Centrepoint and, with the foundation of a safe and stable home, have gone on to establish themselves in their careers, interests and relationships. The night was opened by the London Cabaret Club's resident singer Sofia Klimovsky, who got the crowd in the celebratory mood before the award winners were announced. Videos showcasing the young people's stories brought tears to the eyes of many attendees. The awards included categories like Rising Star, won by a young person whose aim is to build the next unicorn and feature on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list, and the Arts and Educational Excellence Award, won by a young care leaver who has just started his first year at Oxford University studying Philosophy, Politics and Economics. Centrepoint were joined on the evening by some of their longstanding partners, including award sponsors the cardfactory Foundation, ASOS Foundation and Clarksons. Seyi Obakin OBE, Chief Executive at Centrepoint, said: "These awards are a poignant reminder that we are surrounded by talented young people, but the opportunities are not always there or equal. The success of the winners shows what happens when young people are given not just an opportunity to shine, but the support to do it." Following World Homelessness Day last month, contemporary artist Hugh Miller has dedicated his latest oil-on-canvas painting to Centrepoint. (Image: Anne-Marie Doohan) As a young aspiring artist, Hugh did a lot of chalk drawings on pavements near London’s famous landmarks and met inspiring young homeless people along the way. His early years led him to take an interest in the charity’s work. Miller’s Houses of Parliament oil-on-canvas painting is the latest in a series designed to "celebrate the aesthetic beauty of cities in the United Kingdom". The artist was given a rare chance to access the Speaker's Terrace in Parliament last month to complete a section of his painting. The visit attracted the attention of cross-party MPs and raised the profile of Centrepoint and youth homelessness in Parliament. His latest painting - which will take another eight months to finish - will form part of his Centrepoint series collection, with all proceeds from the artwork going to the charity to help end youth homelessness. To find out more about Hugh Miller and his work, visit www.hughmillerart.co.uk Last year, over 118,000 young people faced homelessness. That’s one young person every four minutes. At a time of life when most of their peers are trying new things and taking their first steps into adulthood, these young people found themselves alone and afraid, and unsure where to turn. It doesn’t have to be like this.  With the right support at the right time, these young people can escape homelessness or avoid it altogether. At Centrepoint, we provide more than a bed for the night. We provide a safe place to rebuild, support into education and work, and the confidence to believe in a better future. Youth homelessness is not inevitable. With the right help at the right time, it can be prevented and it can be ended. Our mission is to end youth homelessness – and you can help us. Whether it’s running a marathon or holding a sleep out, you, your friends, family and co-workers can join our movement to end youth homelessness and give vulnerable young people a brighter future. To find out more, donate or get involved, please visit our website http://www.centrepoint.org.uk/newspaper Thirty-seven young people experiencing homelessness had their deaths registered in England and Wales last year, according to the latest figures released by the Office for National Statistics. Of the 37 deaths of young people aged between 16-24 years old, 29 were male and eight were female.  This marks a 2.8% rise from the year before. Overall, 974 people died while experiencing homelessness in England and Wales in 2025.  This marks a 77% increase compared to when the figures were first collated in 2013, rising from 550 to 974.  London had the highest estimated number of deaths in English regions, followed by the North-West and the South-East. Matt Bawden, Director of Progression Housing at Centrepoint said: "Even one death of someone experiencing homelessness is too many. These sobering figures represent countless individual tragedies but are also indicative of a system that is failing. The need to work collaboratively to fix that system and to deliver high-quality housing and support is more urgent than ever.  We believe that every young person should be given the opportunity to lead a fulfilling, healthy life where they can realise their potential."

metadata.title: Andy Burnham hails local news as 'critical' as PM backs Journalism Matters campaign
metadata.contentSnippet: Andy Burnham backs Journalism Matters, calling journalism a vital national infrastructure and local news essential for democracy and accountability.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham hails local news as 'critical' as PM backs Journalism Matters campaign
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Journalism is a vital part of our national infrastructure. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken out in support of the Journalism Matters campaign, emphasising the crucial role of news media in democracy, accountability, and community life. The campaign, coordinated by the News Media Association, highlights the value of journalism and will run from November 2 to 8. Mr Burnham said: "I am proud to support this year's Journalism Matters campaign, which is about recognising journalism not as a nice-to-have, but as part of the national infrastructure of a healthy country and democracy. "It holds power to account, strengthens our resilience and connects people to the places they call home." He stressed the importance of local journalism in the Government’s devolution plans, saying that returning power to communities must go hand in hand with local accountability. Mr Burnham said: "Local reporters are the people sitting in council chambers, courts and planning meetings, asking the questions that need to be asked. "They shine a light on decisions made in people’s name and give communities a voice." He also highlighted the vital role of trusted journalism during times of crisis. Mr Burnham said: "At moments when communities are at their most vulnerable, good local journalism can bring people together and separate fact from fiction. "We saw that after Southport and, more recently, in Belfast, when trusted reporters challenged lies and misinformation being spread online." This year’s Journalism Matters campaign will see the news industry come together to celebrate the role journalism plays underpinning national infrastructure. A recent global report by UNESCO found that countries with a strong, independent press enjoy significant economic and security benefits. News Media Association Chief Executive Theo Bamber (Image: NMA) Theo Bamber, chief executive of the News Media Association, welcomed Mr Burnham’s support but called for practical action. Mr Bamber said: "The Prime Minister is absolutely right to point to the critical role that independent journalism plays in our society and particularly how important local news will be to the success of his own sprawling devolution agenda. "Now, the support shown by the Prime Minister must turn into real action that demonstrates the government understands the changed environment that journalists and news publishers are operating in and strengthens their ability to do more of what they’re brilliant at—chasing stories, uncovering the truth and holding power to account." He called on the Government to protect and promote a diverse media ecosystem. The Journalism Matters campaign runs from November 2 to 8, 2026.

metadata.title: Andy Burnham - 'Journalism is a vital part of our national infrastructure'
metadata.contentSnippet: Prime Minister Andy Burnham explains that with greater local power must come local accountability. And that is why local journalism matters.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham - 'Journalism is a vital part of our national infrastructure'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Too much power in this country has flowed one way: towards Westminster and away from the places where people actually live their lives. This government is changing that. We are putting power and resources back into the hands of communities. Because I want people in local communities to have a bigger say over the decisions that shape their area. But with greater local power must come local accountability. And that is why local journalism matters. Local reporters are the people sitting in council chambers, courts and planning meetings, asking the questions that need to be asked. They shine a light on decisions made in people’s name and give communities a voice. But their role goes much further than holding power to account. At moments when communities are at their most vulnerable, good local journalism can bring people together and separate fact from fiction. We saw that after Southport and, more recently, in Belfast, when trusted reporters challenged lies and misinformation being spread online. And I saw its power myself as Mayor of Greater Manchester. When the Manchester Evening News campaigned for free bus travel for homeless children living in temporary accommodation, it didn't just report what was wrong, it brought people together to get behind the change that was needed. That is exactly what this year's Journalism Matters campaign is about: recognising journalism not as a nice-to-have, but as part of the national infrastructure of a healthy country and democracy. It holds power to account, strengthens our resilience and connects people to the places they call home. And yet access to good local journalism is becoming increasingly unequal. Ninety-five per cent of adults access local news, but the market alone will not sustain it everywhere. Up to 37 local authority districts now have no dedicated outlet of their own, leaving as many as 4.4 million people in local "news deserts", disproportionately in some of our most deprived urban communities. I've spent my career arguing that where you live should not determine the opportunities you get. I believe exactly the same principle applies to information. People in every part of the country deserve trusted local news, scrutiny of those in power and a strong voice for their community. Through our Local Media Action Plan, the new Local News Fund will provide up to £12 million over two years. This is part of a wider package of measures we're delivering to support local journalism. This year, local newspapers, websites and independent television and radio stations in England and Wales have been able to bid for up to £125,000 to invest in their future, whether that's new technology, multimedia journalism, reaching younger audiences or finding new ways to bring in revenue. We have also made up to £275,000 available for projects that strengthen the wider industry. And in the second year, £1 million will help communities bring local journalism back where it has disappeared, whether by reviving a dormant title, expanding a neighbouring publication or establishing a community-owned outlet. We’re doing this because devolution cannot simply mean moving power from one set of politicians to another. It has to mean giving people more of a say. For that to work, they need to know what is being done in their name. They need journalists willing to ask difficult questions, expose wrongdoing, challenge misinformation and champion their communities. That is why I am proud to support this year's Journalism Matters campaign, and why this government will work to ensure trusted local journalism remains at the heart of communities across our country.

metadata.title: Why the UK government must act to protect trusted local journalism
metadata.contentSnippet: Journalism Matters highlights Andy Burnham’s call to protect independent and local news, fair digital markets, and journalism’s role in democracy.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Why the UK government must act to protect trusted local journalism
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Where does a news story come from? A scandal exposed, a failure revealed, a decision brought into the open that someone would rather have kept private. Behind each is work we rarely see. We read the story, take it in and move on. In short, we take journalism for granted. Someone had to find that story, check it, check it again, and then tell it. That takes skill, experience and painstaking work, sometimes over hours, sometimes over days, weeks, months or years. The published story is the bit we all see, and if we want that to continue, we must protect the people and the industry that makes it possible. This year’s Journalism Matters campaign is a chance for us to reflect carefully on what journalism does for all of us, and what we would lose if we didn’t have it. In an article launching this year’s campaign, Prime Minister Andy Burnham cites the enormous benefits that independent journalism delivers for our society and the critical importance of local news media to the devolution agenda. He is absolutely right to do so. Journalism is part of the national infrastructure we all rely on, and the benefits it delivers go far beyond the stories themselves. A global report published by UNESCO earlier this year found a raft of economic and security benefits connected to journalism in countries with an ecosystem which supports an independent free press. So how do we make sure more journalism can happen? It’s clear that there is plenty the government can do to strengthen the conditions that the industry operates in and it must use this opportunity to affect real change. In an article launching this year’s campaign, Prime Minister Andy Burnham cites the enormous benefits that independent journalism delivers for our society and the critical importance of local news media to the devolution agenda (Image: Carlos Jasso/Press Association) This should start with digital markets, and creating an ecosystem which can support and maintain a plural and diverse range of media outlets. This increases user choice and allows publishers that invest in reporting to get a fair return for their work. Meta, always ready and willing to play the role of the tech giant bully, recently launched an assault on journalism with its attempt to force publishers and other businesses to hand over all their content to train its AI products. It was a move right out of the tech platform playbook - bury the crucial detail in a ton of paperwork and then feign disbelief and surprise at the horrified reaction from the business community. This can’t continue and, if the government supports journalism in the way the Prime Minister has outlined, it must back the Competition and Markets Authority to the hilt. The CMA is tasked with making the tech platforms play fair, and to do this job effectively it needs full-throated political support. Nothing else will do. But getting the platforms to play fair is just the start. Government must also make sure that its own policies support journalism, not undermine it. The news prominence regime, as proposed in the Media Green Paper, will have a damaging and distortive effect on the news media landscape if implemented in its current form. Inevitably, local news will be hit particularly hard and the lack of clarity on how platform compliance will be enforced does little to boost our confidence that the policy won’t deliver myriad dangerous, unintended consequences. Ministers must also ensure that the BBC Charter Renewal results in a BBC which partners with the commercial sector rather than competing aggressively against it. And, at a local level, transparency must be maintained as power is shifted out of Westminster to the regions, including by keeping public notices in highly trusted local news media. As the noise around us gets louder and more complex, we still need people intent on establishing the truth. The real, actual truth. This is what journalism does, and this is why bold government support for the industry should be non-negotiable. Without it, we’ll lose our ability to understand the world around us and be consigned to a world where decisions that happen behind closed doors never see the light of day and stories that change lives are never told. That is not an acceptable future for a modern-day democracy such as ours. The Journalism Matters campaign runs from November 2 to 8, 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "leading" UK sports supplement brand has entered administration after 15 years of business. Promuscle Products is based in Fleetwood, Lancashire and was set up in May 2011. It specialises in creating formulas for the sports supplement market for blending, tableting and encapsulation. The company's website states: "Promuscle Products has been leading the way in the sports supplement market for years contract manufacturing some of the biggest brands that have dominated the UK and EU market. "We specialise in creative, innovative formulas and pride ourselves in creating products that a quality assured and taste superb." Promuscle Products also ships out to the USA, Australia and the UAE alongside the UK market. It has 400 ingredients in-house plus over 30 trademarked ingredients they hold the licensees to manufacture. Administrators Philip Lawrence and Gareth Howarth of AMS Business Recovery were appointed on Tuesday, October 27, The Gazette reports. Promuscle Products has been contacted by Newsquest for comment. It has been a tough year for the UK high street, with several retailers entering administration or liquidation and others announcing widespread store closures. Major high street brands Claire's and Quiz have been forced to close all their remaining stores after falling into administration. UK fashion retailer Leading Labels is also set to close its remaining 15 stores after falling into liquidation in May. Whitbread closed all its standalone branded restaurants across the UK last month, affecting five brands: However, Queensway Inns and Common Table Group have now taken over 110 of these former Whitbread sites, saving them from closure. TG Jones and the British Heart Foundation will also be closing around 150 stores each across the UK. Wynsors World of Shoes is shutting 17 stores across the UK, with closing down sales already underway at several affected branches. UK entertainment retailer Zavvi has ceased trading after nearly 20 years, having collapsed into administration for a second time. Australian stationery retailer Typo is also set to pull out of the UK in 2027, closing all its stores and ending online trading. Recommended reading: Meanwhile, UK delivery company Yodel was phased out completely in July after being acquired by InPost. It hasn't all been bad news for the UK high street, with several major brands announcing new store openings for 2026, including Joules, B&M, Aldi, M&S, and Superdrug. Meanwhile, brands including Evans and Bodycare have returned to the UK high street this year after previously closing all their stores. Which business/store closure in 2026 has impacted you the most? metadata.title: One million people warned to act before major UK landline change
metadata.contentSnippet: One million UK households and businesses risk losing landline access as Openreach retires the PSTN.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: One million people warned to act before major UK landline change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: One million people risk losing landline phone access unless they upgrade to digital lines The warning comes as the UK prepares to retire its old analogue phone network and complete the switch to digital lines. BT-owned Openreach are phasing out the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), a system in place since the 1870s, with a full shutdown planned for January 31, 2027. James Lilley, director of customer migrations at Openreach, said: "It’s very hard to get [customers] to read and react and do something." Moving to digital lines is expected to provide a more reliable service, better-quality calls and improved blocking of unwanted calls. Despite these benefits, around one million residents and businesses remain on the old network. Those who do not upgrade in time could lose service or be transferred to a basic emergency phone system without features like voicemail. The UK government says the transition is necessary due to the declining reliability of the copper-based PSTN, and Ofcom has said most users are unlikely to experience significant disruption. The original switch-off date was set for December 31, 2025, but concerns about the impact on vulnerable and rural users, particularly those relying on telecare alarms, led to a revised timeline. Under the PSTN Charter, providers have agreed not to migrate customers using telecare devices unless their equipment is confirmed to be compatible with digital lines. Telecom companies, including BT, are supplying vulnerable customers with free back-up battery packs to ensure phones remain operational during power outages. Unlike the digital system, the traditional PSTN does not depend on mains electricity and will continue to function during a power cut. Openreach has stated that there will not be a single day when all customers lose service. Tens of thousands of customers are reportedly switching to the new system each week, Lilley said a rise in scams had made it harder to get consumers to respond to letters about the change. Have you switched to a digital phone service yet? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Huntingdon tutoring business celebrates 10 years after 100,000 hours of tuition
metadata.contentSnippet: A tutoring business in Huntingdon is celebrating 10 years of supporting students.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon tutoring business celebrates 10 years after 100,000 hours of tuition
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A tutoring business in Huntingdon is celebrating 10 years of supporting students. Tutor Doctor Peterborough Huntingdon Stamford, founded by Piyush Gupta in 2016, has overseen more than 100,000 hours of tuition and helped more than 1,000 young people. Piyush said: "Before this, I worked as an accountant, where success was measured in financial figures. "Now, those numbers are replaced by student outcomes and the difference we’re making to young people’s lives." The business supports children who struggle with mainstream education, including those with special educational needs and mental health difficulties. Piyush recalled the progress of one student who was selective mute, particularly in educational settings. He said: "At the start, they found it a challenge communicating with their tutor. "After several months, they gradually began talking to their peers and became more comfortable around our team and even volunteered to welcome new students." His wife Smita joined the business five years later, bringing more than 20 years of primary education experience. She said: "I’ve never seen Piyush happier in his work, and I’ve learnt so much from him too. "It’s been lovely to bring my expertise into the business in order for us to support even more local students." The couple’s two sons have also been involved, with their eldest now working full-time, making it a true family business. Smita said: "All the relationships we’ve built over the years have been amazing. "Our staff and tutors have been especially important for us, and we couldn’t have achieved what we have done without them." Piyush said he is proud of how far the business has come. He said: "To see where we started, the thought of not being involved anymore is difficult to imagine. "The journey over the past 10 years has been truly amazing."

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire scientist dies in high-speed Spanish train crash
metadata.contentSnippet: A university scientist living in Cambridge has been named as one of 69 people killed in a deadly high-speed train crash in Spain.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire scientist dies in high-speed Spanish train crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A university scientist living in Cambridgeshire has been named as one of 69 people killed in a deadly high-speed train crash in Spain. Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling on one of the trains involved in the collision near Urda, south of Madrid, on Wednesday (October 28). Her death was confirmed by the Centre for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS) three days after the disaster. In a statement posted online, the centre, based in Santiago de Compostela, paid tribute to the "brilliant young researcher". At least 69 people have been killed in the rail disaster (Image: Manu Fernandez/AP) It reads: "The CiMUS community would like to express its support and deepest sympathies to our dear PI María José Alonso, following the death of her niece, Marta Shahbazi, in the railway accident that occurred on 28 October. "Marta was a brilliant young researcher, Group Leader at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology and Affiliate Associate Professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, University of Cambridge. "At this difficult time, we extend our heartfelt condolences to María José and her family, as well as to Marta Shahbazi’s colleagues and collaborators. "Our thoughts are with them all, and we wish them strength and comfort as they come to terms with this profound loss." The 41-year-old had been travelling to receive the scientific excellence prize from the Spanish Society for Developmental Biology. She had been nominated for her research into stem cells and the early stages of human development. Born in Spain, the mum-of-two had been living with her living with her children, aged three and seven, in Cambridge. Authorities have since blamed the crash on a computer failure and human error. (Image: Juanma Jimenez/Europa Press via AP) Dr Shahbazi began her career at the Autonomous University of Madrid where she received an undergraduate degree in Biology. She also received an MSc in Molecular Biomedicine before obtaining her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre. In 2019, she received the 3Rs Prize for "providing an opportunity to replace and reduce the use of mice in developmental biology studies." The affiliate associate professor at the University of Cambridge led a group of researchers at the MCR Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB). The Laboratory had previously confirmed Dr Shahbazi was on one of the trains but said here whereabouts were "unknown". In a tribute on its website, the LMB said it is "deeply saddened" by the "tragic death" of the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist". "Her death is a profound shock and a huge loss. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time. "The LMB is offering support to members of its community as they navigate this tragic loss." The collision occurred when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company. It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Authorities have since blamed the crash on a computer failure and human error. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: If you're looking for a "traditional" pub serving "sensational" food in Cambridgeshire, then look no further. With its exposed beams, varied furnishings and large inglenook fireplace, The White Horse, in Eaton Socon, has been described as "nice and cosy". On its website, the venue proudly describes how it "pairs centuries-old character with a relaxed, modern pub experience". The former coaching inn was given a new lease of life thanks to its new owners Kerry and Simon Smith. They worked around the clock for more than five weeks to renovate The White Horse in time for its grand reopening in October last year. According to Mrs Smith, the pair had spent "12-hour days" trying to get the pub up to standard, including work to the kitchen and interior. The couple hoped to create a pub that is part of the community, turning their attention to the pub's exterior and garden. Naturally, The White Horse has received raving reviews on Trip Advisor, with visitors praising its "excellent, accommodating staff". One visitor said: "Real value for money and my husband had the Korean crispy chicken burger which he thought was absolutely sensational." The White Horse dates back to the 1700s and the new owners are bringing it back to life as a “true village pub". Whether you're dropping in for a pint, meeting friends or enjoying a roast, "you'll find honest food and genuine hospitality," its website reads. Centred around fresh ingredients, the menu boasts classic British favourites and "hearty plates". It adds: "From Sunday roasts to seasonal dishes and pub staples, everything is prepared with the care you’d expect from a family-run kitchen." "We’re creating a community-focused pub where everyone feels at home." "Expect good food, friendly faces, and regular events — all in a space that celebrates the history and heart of Eaton Socon." metadata.title: Historic railway bridge murals celebrating area's past given the green light
metadata.contentSnippet: Murals celebrating the former railway line between Brampton and Grafham have been approved for a disused Grafham Road bridge by Huntingdonshire District Council.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Historic railway bridge murals celebrating area's past given the green light
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Two murals celebrating a former railway line have been approved for a disused bridge between Brampton and Grafham. Huntingdonshire District Council has granted advertisement consent for the artwork on the underside of the railway bridge on Grafham Road, Brampton. The decision was issued today (Friday). The two murals will each measure approximately 2.5 metres high by four metres wide and will be painted directly onto the underside of the bridge. Historic railway bridge murals celebrating area's past given the green light. (Image: HDC) The designs will feature predominantly cream text against a dark blue background, with the colours chosen to reflect the historic railway livery associated with the former line. The bridge is on a designated Quiet Road between Brampton and Grafham, surrounded by agricultural fields to the south and Brampton Wood to the north. Planning officers said the artwork had been designed to reflect the historic significance of the former railway and would provide a “cultural and heritage reference” sympathetic to the character of the area. Historic railway bridge murals celebrating area's past given the green light. (Image: HDC) They added that because of the murals’ scale, location and appearance, they would not harm the visual amenity of the area. Cambridgeshire's Highway Authority raised no objections to the plans, noting that the murals would be static and would not include illuminated, moving or digital elements which could distract road users. Officers also noted that the Quiet Road is characterised by lower vehicle speeds and is shared by pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and motorists. No objections from members of the public were received during consideration of the application. The council concluded that the murals were of an appropriate scale and design and would not have a significantly detrimental impact on the area's appearance or harm public or highway safety. Formal consent has now been granted subject to conditions, including that the artwork is maintained so it does not impair the visual amenity of the site or endanger the public. The advertisement consent lasts for five years from the date of the decision. The Brampton-to-Grafham route forms part of the National Cycle Network and was considered for designation as Cambridgeshire's first Quiet Lane.

metadata.title: Are you owed £8,000? HMRC is sending out 311,000 new letters to people due money
metadata.contentSnippet: Thousands of people - mostly mums - are due money back from historic State Pension errors, as HMRC has sent out 311,000 letters to people who could be missing out.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Are you owed £8,000? HMRC is sending out 311,000 new letters to people due money
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of people - mostly mums - are due money back from historic State Pension errors, as HMRC has sent out 311,000 letters to people who could be missing out. The letters are aimed at parents and carers who may be missing Home Responsibilities Protection (HRP) from their National Insurance records, potentially leaving them with a lower State Pension than they should receive. HMRC says the latest mailout will run until the end of March 2027, with 215,000 letters going to people who have already reached State Pension age. The department says the letters will include a claim form for the first time, making it easier for people to apply for HRP without having to download or print the paperwork themselves. Official figures show that more than 25,000 people have had HRP added to their National Insurance records since HMRC began sending letters in September 2023. Nearly all were above State Pension age, and they have received a share of more than £100million in pension arrears. The average arrears payment has been around £8,000, although the amount an individual receives depends on their circumstances and whether they are eligible. Home Responsibilities Protection was introduced to help protect the State Pension entitlement of parents and carers who took time away from paid employment to raise children or care for others. People who claimed Child Benefit between 1978 and May 2000 may be affected if HRP is missing from their National Insurance records. During this period, people claiming Child Benefit were not always required to provide their National Insurance number. HMRC says that while HRP was automatically added to the records of people who supplied their NI number, some people who did not provide it may have missed out. HRP reduced the number of qualifying years a person needed on their National Insurance record to receive a full basic State Pension. The scheme was replaced by National Insurance credits in 2010, meaning people who started claiming Child Benefit after that date will not be affected by this particular issue. HMRC and the Department for Work and Pensions have been contacting people who may be missing HRP for the past three years. The department says it has already sent 340,000 letters inviting people to check whether they qualify. Following a successful trial of a revised letter, a further 311,000 are being sent out by next March. The latest letters will include the CF411 claim form, which recipients can complete with their personal details and return by post. HMRC says checking eligibility online remains the quickest option for people who can use the service. Claimants can use the GOV.UK eligibility tool to check whether they may be missing HRP and submit a claim online. Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer, said: “We're hopeful that by including the claim form in the letter, people are more likely to fill it in, send it back and find out quickly and easily whether their entitlement will increase on retirement or, if they've reached State Pension age, they're owed a payout.” Pensioners with income up to the value of the full new state pension (to be £13,040 from April 2027) will not pay tax. Mechanism not stated, I suspect there will be an effective increased pensioner allowance with a clawback for income above that. More when I know more. #Budget2026 — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) October 28, 2026 HMRC says people do not need to use a third-party company to check their eligibility or submit an application, meaning they can avoid paying a firm a share of any arrears they receive. Anyone who needs help can call the National Insurance Helpline on 0300 200 3500. Further support is also available online. Research published by the Department for Work and Pensions in May 2025, based on work carried out by Verian, examined why some people did not respond to the earlier campaign. The research identified several possible reasons, including fears that letters could be scams, confusion about the terminology used and uncertainty about whether the recipient was eligible for money. Some people struggled to understand how HRP related to their own circumstances. Others were concerned that making a claim could leave them worse off or lacked confidence in completing the process online. The findings highlight the challenge of reaching people who may be entitled to arrears but do not realise that the letters apply to them. Elaine Walker, director of AskRose, said: “The government's own research tells us exactly why so many people didn't respond last time. "Letters didn't arrive, people didn't think they applied to them, they couldn't see what they stood to gain, and many understandably feared the letter was a scam.” Recommended reading: HMRC is encouraging people who have retired or are approaching retirement to check their National Insurance records for gaps that could affect their State Pension entitlement. The main steps are: Not everyone who checks their record will be entitled to arrears. The amount, if any, will depend on their National Insurance history and individual circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Wrong council tax band? What it could mean for your £100 bank energy payment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Around 20 million households will receive a £100 energy payment this winter under plans announced by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget. Households in council tax bands A to D in England are expected to receive the money through the council tax system from January 2027, most likely paid directly into their bank accounts, according to Martin Lewis. The scheme will cost £2.6 billion, with funding also being provided to devolved administrations so they can introduce similar support elsewhere in the UK. Mr Healey said the payment would help families cope with rising energy bills during the coldest months. He told the Commons: “This winter, for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D, I am announcing a £100 energy payment for households, paid directly into people’s bank accounts to deal with rising energy bills. “That’s a £2.6 billion scheme to take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people though to the spring.” Mr Healey urged devolved administrations to “do the same and give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter”. But how can you tell if you are eligible for the £100 payment, and what happens if you think you are in the wrong Council Tax band? It's not clear what the deadline will be for this yet, but Martin Lewis has previously shared his advice about what to do if you think your council tax bill is too high. The consumer champion explained how two simple checks can lower your Council Tax bill this year and forever - but it has to be done with care. He explained: "Up to 400,000 people in England and Scotland are in the wrong band, a higher band, and I've been looking at how you can challenge this since 2007. "Effectively, what you need to do is go onto voa.gov.uk to check your council tax band of an identical property, or if it's Scotland, saa.gov.uk. "If you're in a higher band, the name is in identical properties, then you need to work out what bad you would have been in 1991 if that shows you had a band. "Then you need to look at going forward to get your band lower." 'What can you do if your council tax is going up?' - @susannareid100@MartinSLewis explains what you can do, as he points out that many people could be missing out on discounts. pic.twitter.com/VkucbcAS2K — Good Morning Britain (@GMB) April 1, 2025 Council tax bands were drawn up in 1991 based on drive-by valuations of homes at that time. They are subsequently out of date and many people may actually be in the wrong council tax band. In 2007, financial expert and Money Saving Expert founder Martin Lewis started a campaign to show how you might be able to challenge it. The Check and Challenge approach made huge headlines that year and many people have been able to use it to save themselves money since then. Here’s how it works: You can find out more about Martin Lewis' method - read it carefully before making any challenge. The Check and Challenge method has two steps, and it is absolutely vital you do both before deciding whether to get your council tax banding assessed. Step one involves finding out if your band is higher than neighbours in similar or identical properties. Thankfully, this is public information, so you don’t need to go and ask them. England valuation bands are listed here, and the valuations are here. The band of every property in Scotland can be found on the Scottish Assessors Association website. All domestic properties in Wales are put into 9 tax bands (bands A to I). The tax bands are based on how much a home and the land it is on is worth. The Valuation Office Agency (VOA) values properties for Council Tax purposes. They are the government's property experts for Wales and England. When comparing your band with your neighbours’, make sure the properties are as close in size and value as possible, and would have been in 1991. If neighbours in similar properties are in a lower band than you, then you may have a claim. However, you could land yourself in bother if you don’t do the next step. If your band is different to your neighbours’ and you’re in similar properties, then it could be that their band is wrong and not yours, and you could actually end up landing them with a larger bill if you appeal - you risk becoming an unpopular neighbour. So here is an important next step before deciding to challenge… A second crucial step is to estimate what your home was worth in 1991, as that's when and how the council tax bands were defined. If you bought your house after 1991, you can simply use its price and date of sale to do this. If you rent or bought earlier, you'll need to find an estimated price. It's also worth doing this with similar neighbouring properties. To find a price quickly, you can use a website which offers free historic sales price information such as Zoopla or Rightmove. Enter your street name and it'll tell you the prices of all properties sold there since 2000. Find the most recent sale price of a similar property to yours in your street. Now note down both the price and the date of sale. Once you have that information, you can use it to estimate what your property would've been worth back in 1991, and what band it's in. There is a calculator you can use here, which uses house price data from Nationwide. Recommended reading: This will only give a rough indication, but it gives an idea. You may be in a higher band than your neighbours because they’re in the wrong band, not you. In that case, if you appeal and stay in the same band, but their band is increased, you might not make many friends. Now you've worked out roughly what your property was worth in 1991, you can compare this to a table here to see what band you should have been put in, based on that home value. If you're convinced your property band is unfair after all the checks, you could challenge it. In Scotland, the SAA deals with council tax bands. Enter your postcode in the council tax bands search box on the homepage. Select your property from the list. If you want to challenge the banding, click on "Make a proposal". You can then fill in an online form which will be sent to your local assessor, who will contact you. But do remember, you can’t just ask for your band to be lowered, only for it to be reassessed, which means it could be moved up or down. This is why it’s important to do both checks and think about whether you’ve added an extension to your home or bought extra land or outbuildings.

metadata.title: Drivers warned over viral fuel-saving petrol pump trick that experts say won't work
metadata.contentSnippet: Fuel-saving ‘slow squeeze’ hack debunked by expert, who warns UK motorists it will not cut petrol or diesel costs; repeated topping off can damage vehicles.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drivers warned over viral fuel-saving petrol pump trick that experts say won't work
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A motoring expert has debunked a viral fuel-saving tip making the rounds on social media. The so-called "slow squeeze" method, gaining traction on TikTok and Instagram, claims that gently squeezing the fuel pump trigger while filling up will get motorists more petrol or diesel for their money by reducing air bubbles and foam in the tank. The theory has gained attention online, with one TikTok post under the tag "Fuel Prices UK" reaching almost 250,000 views. However, Graham Conway, managing director at Select Car Leasing, said the advice is misguided and unlikely to deliver any real benefit. Mr Conway said: "The ‘slow squeeze’ hack is popular on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, but you’re highly unlikely to see any real benefit. "Modern fuel pumps have clever systems designed to prevent air or vapour from affecting the measurement of fuel that comes out of the nozzle. "You can’t somehow game the system with the trickle method. "The only thing that might happen is that you take ages to fill up, angering other drivers patiently waiting behind you." The creator of the trend argued that filling up too quickly creates bubbles in the tank, similar to pouring a fizzy drink too fast. Despite Mr Conway’s explanation, some social media users remain convinced the method works. One commenter said: "I always fill up holding the lever halfway and my petrol lasts way longer. "By holding the lever in all the way in we are paying for a lot of air too." Another claimed that it could "make a litre or two difference in a fill up." Mr Conway also used the opportunity to warn against another common mistake at the pump: topping off the tank after the nozzle clicks. He said: "Squeezing the fuel pump trigger after the nozzle has automatically clicked off, also known as ‘topping off,’ might seem like a sensible way to squeeze a little extra fuel into your tank. "But doing so repeatedly could actually end up damaging your car, potentially leaving you facing an expensive repair bill. "Most modern petrol cars are fitted with an evaporative emissions control system, which captures petrol vapours from the fuel tank and stores them in a charcoal canister, preventing them from escaping into the atmosphere. "However, if you continue forcing petrol into an already full tank, liquid fuel can enter parts of this system that are designed to handle vapour rather than liquid. "This can damage the charcoal canister and other components, potentially triggering an engine management warning light and even contributing to an MOT failure. "Although diesel vehicles generally don't use the same charcoal-canister system, overfilling can still cause fuel to spill or interfere with the tank's venting arrangements. "Repairs to a damaged evaporative emissions system can run into hundreds of pounds, depending on the vehicle and the extent of the damage. "So, while an occasional extra squeeze isn't guaranteed to cause problems, it's best to stop filling when the nozzle automatically clicks off. "That way, you can avoid the risk of an unnecessary repair bill." The warnings come as UK motorists continue to look for ways to cut costs at the pump amid persistently high fuel prices. Have you ever tried this 'slow squeeze' method before? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: The best woodland walks in Cambridgeshire to discover this autumn
metadata.contentSnippet: From ancient woodlands and National Trust estates to wildlife-rich nature reserves, Cambridgeshire offers far more woodland scenery than many people realise.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The best woodland walks in Cambridgeshire to discover this autumn
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From ancient woodlands and National Trust estates to wildlife-rich nature reserves, Cambridgeshire offers far more woodland scenery than many people realise. Showcasing some of the county's most attractive forest and woodland walks, here are six beauty spots to discover this autumn. While best known for its wetlands, Wicken Fen also contains areas of woodland and scrub that create a wonderfully varied walking experience. The reserve's network of paths passes through reedbeds, grassland and developing woodland, offering visitors the chance to spot everything from dragonflies and marsh harriers to grazing Konik ponies. The ever-changing landscape and huge skies make every walk feel different, whatever the season. One of the county's most important ancient woodlands, Monk's Wood is a haven for wildlife and a favourite among walkers seeking tranquillity. The reserve's oak and ash trees line peaceful trails that weave through centuries-old woodland. During spring, woodland flowers brighten the forest floor, while birdwatchers can enjoy sightings of woodpeckers, nuthatches and other woodland species. The largest country estate in Cambridgeshire offers far more than historic architecture. Its extensive parkland includes pockets of mature woodland, tree-lined avenues and scenic walking routes stretching across the estate. Visitors can wander beneath ancient trees before emerging into open countryside with far-reaching views. Managed by the National Trust, it combines woodland beauty with some of the county's most impressive landscapes. Famous for its gardens, Anglesey Abbey also boasts beautiful woodland walks that are particularly spectacular during autumn. Shaded paths wind through mature trees and carefully designed landscapes, creating a peaceful retreat from nearby Cambridge. Seasonal colour is a major draw, while the estate's varied habitats support a wide range of birds and other wildlife. It is one of the most picturesque places for a gentle woodland stroll in the county. Covering more than 170 acres, Hinchingbrooke Country Park combines mature woodland with lakes, meadows and open countryside. Well-maintained trails guide visitors through shady woodland areas rich in birdlife and seasonal wildflowers. The park's accessibility and variety of routes make it popular with families, dog walkers and runners alike, while its peaceful setting provides a welcome escape from nearby Huntingdon. One of Cambridgeshire's most diverse nature reserves, Paxton Pits features woodland trails alongside lakes, meadows and wetlands. The reserve is particularly popular with wildlife enthusiasts thanks to its rich birdlife and varied habitats. Visitors can enjoy peaceful woodland walks before exploring the waterside paths and observation points. At Paxton Pits, the Heron Trail and Meadow Trail offer opportunities to spot wildlife around the reserve's lakes as the seasons change. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: The stunning National Trust site in Cambridgeshire perfect for a day out
metadata.contentSnippet: Tucked away on the banks of the River Great Ouse, Houghton Mill is home stunning scenery and wildlife-rich habitats.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The stunning National Trust site in Cambridgeshire perfect for a day out
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Tucked away on the banks of the River Great Ouse, this National Trust site is among Cambridgeshire's underrated attractions. Overshadowed by some of the region's larger historic sites, this riverside retreat combines heritage, wildlife and scenic walking routes. At the heart of the site is Houghton Mill, the last surviving working watermill on the River Great Ouse. Visitors can explore the historic building and discover how grain was transformed into flour using traditional machinery, with volunteer millers helping bring centuries of history to life. During the operating season, the giant waterwheel can still be seen turning, offering a glimpse into a way of life that once powered communities across the country. Beyond the mill lies the beautiful Waterclose Meadows, a landscape of riverside grassland, wildlife-rich habitats and tranquil walking paths. Footpaths lead through the meadows and along the river towards the picturesque villages of The Hemingfords, making it a favourite spot for walkers, photographers and nature lovers. In summer, the meadows buzz with insects and birds, while the river provides a constantly changing backdrop. Despite its rural atmosphere, visitors will find plenty of amenities. The on-site tea room enjoys a picturesque riverside location and serves freshly made cakes, scones, light lunches, hot drinks and seasonal treats. Indoor and outdoor seating allows visitors to relax beside the water after exploring the site. There is also parking, a gift shop, toilet facilities and accessible routes around much of the property. Families are well catered for, with open green spaces, picnic areas and easy riverside walks providing plenty of opportunities to enjoy the outdoors together. The site is also popular with cyclists thanks to nearby links with the wider cycle network. For those looking to discover a quieter side of Cambridgeshire, Houghton Mill and Waterclose Meadows offers history, scenery and relaxation in equal measure. It may be one of the county's hidden gems, but once visited, it is unlikely to remain a secret for long. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Village’s only café scales back hours
metadata.contentSnippet: The Cherry Branch café in Cherry Hinton has been warned it will "run out of money" if it doesn’t make major changes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Village’s only café scales back hours
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridge village’s only café has been warned it will ‘run out of money’ if it doesn’t make major changes. The Cherry Branch café in Cherry Hinton has faced major finanial issues in its first year. Cambridge City Council owns the building, which includes the library, with the kitchen, café and meeting rooms rented by the charity Cherry Hinton Community Benefit Society (CHCBS). Kate Jones, one of the cafe’s trustees, said a business consultant told them, “there’s no two ways about it – you’re going to run out of money”. The 51-year-old said: “It’s difficult when something like this happens – which nobody wanted – and understandably people were upset.” The group said they were required to pay a facilities management charge of £32,000 per year as part of the lease agreement with the city council. This covered building maintenance such as cleaning, gardening and repairs but left the group unable to hire their own contractors meaning they had to do some tasks themselves. Ms Jones said: “That contract meant we were paying a lot of money as a small charity, bearing in mind this is our first year.” The CHCBS also hired a catering manager as a contractor instead of an employee – which would have been cheaper – as they said the council wanted their contract to be terminated more easily if the lease ended. They said the fees for this on top of the facilities management charge were too much as they could only make money from café sales and hiring out meeting rooms. The group took the decision to end the catering manager’s contract and the council has frozen the facilities management charge until March 2027. Ms Jones said: “What we were finding was trustees were doing day to day work in the hub – including the chair actually cleaning the toilets. That meant our ability to have that thinking time was taken away – every time there’s a regular booking someone needs to be here. Now we need to focus on making the hub sustainable – the council have been super helpful and have offered us a hub manager.” The cafe will now be able to stay open with scaled back hours after closing temporarily. A meeting was held this month to reassure Cherry Hinton residents that it is not closing. Ms Jones added: “I think the meeting was good because we were able to just address some of the things people had heard that weren’t right. “We wanted to reassure people the hub is still here, the café is still open, and the trustees are absolutely committed and working extremely hard to deliver this community facility to the people of Cherry Hinton.” Cllr Mike Todd-Jones, the council’s cabinet member for communities, said: “I’m determined to work in partnership with the Cherry Hinton Community Benefit Society to help put the Hub on a sustainable financial footing for the future. “Through workshops with the CHCBS, and support from local councillors and the council team, we will work hard together to develop a plan that means the Hub will be in a strong position to serve the people of Cherry Hinton for many years to come.” Be sure to set CambridgeshireLive as your preferred news source to make sure you never miss a story. Simply click here and tick the box. A spokesperson for Cambridge City Council said they were helping to support the CHCBS “through this tricky period”. They said: “Cherry Hinton Hub and Library is a vital focus for the local community and Cambridge City Council is fully committed to its success having redeveloped the former library at a cost of over £1.5 million – funding from the City Council and S106 developer contributions. “The first year or two operating a community facility and establishing a café can be really tough. Maximising income from room hire and the café in this early period is difficult and, combined with the expenses associated with opening new premises, this has proved financially challenging. “The city council has already stepped in to support the CHCBS, suspending facilities management charges from June 2026 to March 2027 alongside other financial help that should save CHCBS around £30,000. The city council is also proposing to pay for an interim Hub manager.” The cafe will be open from 10am to 2pm on Wednesdays only.

metadata.title: The picturesque Cambridgeshire village that feels frozen in time
metadata.contentSnippet: Just a couple of miles from the centre of Cambridge, Grantchester offers a rare combination of countryside tranquillity and city convenience.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The picturesque Cambridgeshire village that feels frozen in time
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Just a couple of miles from the centre of Cambridge, this picturesque village offers a rare combination of countryside tranquillity and city convenience. Frequently rated among the best places to live in Cambridgeshire, the village boasts beautiful surroundings and feels frozen in time. It has a strong community spirit and easy access to some of the county's most famous green spaces. Set on the banks of the River Cam, Grantchester feels a world away from the bustle of city life. The village is surrounded by open countryside, grazing land and the renowned Grantchester Meadows. The meadows have inspired poets and visitors for generations and remain one of the area's biggest attractions today. Despite its peaceful character, Grantchester boasts a selection of well-loved amenities. Among the most famous is The Orchard Tea Garden, which has been serving visitors since 1897 and remains a favourite spot for afternoon tea beneath fruit trees. The village is also home to traditional pubs including The Red Lion and The Green Man, both of which draw locals and tourists looking for classic food and drinks. Grantchester has long been associated with literary figures including Rupert Brooke, while its centuries-old Church of St Andrew & St Mary stands at the heart of the community. The village gained international recognition through the ITV drama Grantchester, which introduced its idyllic streets to television audiences around the world. For those seeking a quintessential English village experience, Grantchester delivers in abundance. With historic pubs, charming architecture and a setting that feels timeless, it is easy to see why so many people consider this riverside gem a must-visit location.
